In [[quantum probability]], the '''Belavkin equation''', also known as '''Belavkin-Schrödinger equation''', '''quantum filtering equation''', '''stochastic master equation''', is a quantum stochastic differential equation describing the dynamics of a [[quantum system]] undergoing observation in continuous time.  It was derived and henceforth studied by [[Viacheslav Belavkin]] in 1988.<ref name="Belavkin88">{{cite book
 | last = Belavkin | first = V.P.
 | chapter = Nondemolition measurements, nonlinear filtering and dynamic programming of quantum stochastic processes
 | editor = A. Blaquiere
 | title = Proc of Bellmann Continuum Workshop 'Modelling and Control of Systems'
 | place = Sophia-Antipolis
 | volume = 121
 | series = Lecture notes in Control and Inform Sciences
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | year = 1988
 | pages = 245–265
}}</ref><ref name="Belavkin89a">{{cite journal
 | last = Belavkin | first = V.P.
 | title = A continuous counting observation and posterior quantum dynamics
 | journal = J Phys A
 | volume = 22
 | issue = 23
 | year = 1989
 | pages = L1109–L1114
 | doi = 10.1088/0305-4470/22/23/006
|bibcode = 1989JPhA...22L1109B }}</ref><ref name="Belavkin89b">{{cite journal
 | last = Belavkin | first = V.P.
 | title = A new wave equation for a continuous nondemolition measurement
 | journal = Physics Letters A
 | volume = 140
 | issue = 7–8
 | year = 1989
 | pages = 355–358
 | doi = 10.1016/0375-9601(89)90066-2
|bibcode = 1989PhLA..140..355B | arxiv = quant-ph/0512136| s2cid = 6083856
 }}</ref>

==Overview==
Unlike the [[Schrödinger equation]], which describes the deterministic evolution of the [[wavefunction]] <math>\psi(t)</math> of a closed system (without interaction), the Belavkin equation describes the stochastic evolution of a random wavefunction <math>\psi(t,\omega)</math> of an [[open quantum system]] interacting with an observer:
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title= 
|equation = :<math>d\psi=-\left(\frac{1}{2} L^\ast L+\frac{i}{\hbar}H\right)\psi dt+L\psi dy</math>
|cellpadding= 6 
|border 
|border colour = #0073CF 
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}

Here, <math>L</math> is a [[self-adjoint operator]] (or a column vector of operators) of the system coupled to the external field, <math>H</math> is the Hamiltonian, <math>i=\sqrt{-1}</math> is the imaginary unit, <math>\hbar</math> is the [[Planck constant]], and <math>y(t)=\int_0^t dy(r)</math> is a [[stochastic process]] representing the measurement noise that is a martingale with [[independent increments]] with respect to the input probability measure <math>P(0,d\omega)=\|\psi(0,\omega)\|^2\mu(d\omega)</math>.  Note that this noise has dependent increments with respect to the output probability measure <math>P(t,d\omega)=\|\psi(t,\omega)\|^2\mu(d\omega)</math> representing the output innovation process (the observation).  For <math>L=0</math>, the equation becomes the standard [[Schrödinger equation]].

The stochastic process <math>y(t)</math> can be a mixture of two basic types: the ''Poisson'' (or ''jump'') type <math>y(t)\simeq n(t)-t</math>, where <math>n(t)</math> is a [[Poisson process]] corresponding to counting observation, and the ''Brownian'' (or ''diffusion'') type <math>y(t)\simeq w(t)</math>, where <math>w(t)</math> is the standard [[Wiener process]] corresponding to continuous observation.  The equations of the diffusion type can be derived as the central limit of the jump type equations with the expected rate of the jumps increasing to infinity.

The random wavefunction <math>\psi(t,\omega)</math> is normalized only in the mean-squared sense <math>\int\|\psi(t,\omega)\|^2\mu(d\omega)=\|\psi_0\|=1</math>, but generally <math>\psi(t,\omega)</math> fails to be normalized for each <math>\omega</math>.  The normalization of <math>\psi(t,\omega)</math> for each <math>\omega</math> gives the random ''posterior state vector'' <math>\varphi(t,\omega)=\psi(t,\omega)/\|\psi(t,\omega)\|</math>, the evolution of which is described by the posterior Belavkin equation, which is nonlinear, because operators <math>L</math> and <math>H</math> depend on <math>\varphi</math> due to normalization.  The stochastic process <math>y(t)</math> in the posterior equation has independent increments with respect to the output probability measure <math>P(t,d\omega)=\|\psi(t,\omega)\|^2\mu(d\omega)</math>, but not with respect to the input measure.  Belavkin also derived linear equation for unnormalized density operator <math>\varrho(t,\omega)=\psi(t,\omega)\psi^\ast(t,\omega)</math> and the corresponding nonlinear equation for the normalized random posterior density operator <math>\rho(t,\omega)=\varphi(t,\omega)\varphi^\ast(t,\omega)</math>.  For two types of measurement noise, this gives eight basic quantum stochastic differential equations.  The general forms of the equations include all types of noise and their representations in [[Fock space]].<ref name="Belavkin95">{{cite journal
 | last = Belavkin | first = V.P.
 | title = On stochastic generators of completely positive cocycles
 | journal = Russ Journ of Math Phys
 | volume = 3
 | number = 4
 | year = 1995
 | pages = 523–528
}}</ref>
<ref name="Belavkin97">{{cite journal
 | last = Belavkin | first = V.P.
 | title = Quantum stochastic positive evolutions: characterization, construction, dilation
 | journal = Commun. Math. Phys.
 | volume = 184
 | issue = 3
 | year = 1997
 | pages = 533–566
 | doi = 10.1007/s002200050072
|arxiv = math-ph/0512042 |bibcode = 1997CMaPh.184..533B | s2cid = 17593922
 }}</ref>

The nonlinear equation describing observation of position of a free particle, which is a special case of the posterior Belavkin equation of the diffusion type, was also obtained by Diosi<ref name="Diosi89">{{cite journal
 | last = Di'osi | first = L.
 | title = Models for universal reduction of macroscopic quantum fluctuations
 | journal =  Physical Review A
 | volume = 40
 | issue = 3
 | year = 1989
 | pages = 1165–1174
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevA.40.1165
| pmid = 9902248
 |bibcode = 1989PhRvA..40.1165D }}</ref> and appeared in the works of Gisin,<ref name="Gisin89">{{cite journal
 | last = Gisin | first = N.
 | title = Stochastic quantum dynamics and relativity
 | journal = Helvetica Physica Acta
 | volume = 62
 | year = 1989
 | pages = 363–371
}}</ref> Ghirardi, Pearle and Rimini,<ref name="Ghirardi_etal1990">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Ghirardi | first1 = G.C.
 | last2 = Pearle | first2 = P.
 | last3 = Rimini | first3 = A.
 | title = Markov processes in Hilbert space and continuous spontaneous localization of systems of identical particles
 | journal = Phys. Rev. A
 | volume = 42
 | issue = 1
 | year = 1990
 | pages = 78–89
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevA.42.78
| pmid = 9903779
 |bibcode = 1990PhRvA..42...78G }}</ref> although with a rather different motivation or interpretation.  Similar nonlinear equations for posterior density operators were postulated (although without derivation) in quantum optics and the quantum trajectories theory,<ref name="Carmichael93">{{cite book
 | last = Carmichael | first = H.J.
 | title = An Open Systems Approach to Quantum Optics
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | year = 1993
}}</ref> where they are called ''stochastic master equations''.  The averaging of the equations for the random density operators <math>\rho(t,\omega)</math> over all random trajectories <math>\omega</math> leads to the [[Lindblad equation]],<ref name="Smolyanov-Truman99">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Smolyanov | first1 = O.
 | last2 = Truman | first2 = A.
 | title = Schrödinger-Belavkin equations and associated Kolmogorov and Lindblad equations
 | journal = Theoretical and Mathematical Physics
 | volume = 120
 | number = 2
 | year = 1999
 | pages = 973–984
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02557405
|bibcode = 1999TMP...120..973S | s2cid = 121436901
 }}</ref> which is deterministic.

The nonlinear Belavkin equations for posterior states play the same role as the Stratonovich–[[Kushner equation]] in classical probability, while the linear equations correspond to the [[Zakai equation]].<ref name="Holevo91">{{cite book
 | last = Holevo | first = A.S.
 | chapter = Quantum probability and quantum statistics
 | editor = Prokhorov, Y.V.
 | title = Probability Theory~8
 | volume = 83
 | series = Itogi Nauki i Tekhniki
 | publisher = VINITI
 | year = 1991
 | pages = 5–132
 | language = ru
 | url = http://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=intf&paperid=209&what=fullt&option_lang=eng
}}</ref>  The Belavkin equations describe continuous-time [[decoherence]] of initially pure state <math>\rho(0)=\psi_0\psi_0^\ast</math> into a mixed posterior state <math>\rho(t)=\int\varphi(t,\omega)\varphi^\ast(t,\omega)P(t,d\omega)</math> giving a rigorous description of the dynamics of the wavefunction collapse due to an observation or measurement.<ref name="Belavkin90">{{cite book

 | title = Stochastics and Quantum Mechanics
 | publisher = World Scientific

 | pages = 40–68
}}</ref>
<ref name="Belavkin92">{{cite journal

 | title = Quantum continual measurements and a posteriori collapse on CCR.
 | journal = Comm. Math. Phys.
 | volume = 146

 | pages = 611–635

|arxiv = math-ph/0512070 |bibcode = 1992CMaPh.146..611B | s2cid = 17016809
 }}</ref>

 }}</ref>

== Non-demolition measurement and quantum filtering ==
Noncommutativity presents a major challenge for probabilistic interpretation of quantum stochastic differential equations due to non-existence of conditional expectations for general pairs of quantum observables.  Belavkin resolved this issue by discovering the error-perturbation uncertainty relation and formulating the non-demolition principle of quantum measurement.<ref name="Belavkin92" /><ref name="Belavkin80">{{cite book
 | last = Belavkin | first = V.P.
 | title = Quantum Communications and Measurement
 | chapter = Quantum Filtering of Markov Signals with White Quantum Noise
 | volume = 25
 | year = 1980
 | pages = 1445–1453
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4899-1391-3_37
 | arxiv = quant-ph/0512091
| isbn = 978-1-4899-1393-7
 | s2cid = 15021588
 }}</ref>  In particular, if the stochastic process <math>dy(t)</math> corresponds to the error <math>e(t)dt=dw</math> (white noise in the diffusive case) of a noisy observation <math>Y(t)=X(t)+e(t)</math> of operator <math>X(t)=\lambda[L(t)+L^\ast(t)]</math> with the accuracy coefficient <math>\lambda>0</math>, then the indirect observation perturbs the dynamics of the system by a stochastic force <math>f(t)</math>, called the ''Langevin force'', which is another white noise of intensity <math>(\hbar\lambda)^2</math> that does not commute with the error <math>e(t)</math>.  The result of such a perturbation is that the output process <math>Y(t)</math> is commutative <math>[Y(s),Y(t)]=0</math>, and hence <math>\int_0^tY(r)dr</math> corresponds to a classical observation, while the system operators <math>X</math> satisfy the non-demolition condition: all future observables must commute with the past observations (but not with the future observations): <math>[X(s),Y(t)]=0</math> for all <math>s\geq t</math> (but not <math>s<t</math>).  Note that commutation of <math>X(s)</math> with <math>Y(t)</math> and another operator <math>Z(s)</math> with <math>Y(t)</math> does not imply commutation of <math>X(s)</math> with <math>Z(s)</math>, so that the algebra of future observables is still non-commutative.  The non-demolition condition is necessary and sufficient for the existence of conditional expectations <math>\mathbb{E}\{X(s)\mid Y(t)\}</math>, which makes the quantum filtering possible.<ref name="Bouten_etal09">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Bouten | first1 = L.
 | last2 = van Handel | first2 = R.
 | last3 = James | first3 = M.R.
 | title = A discrete invitation to quantum filtering and feedback control
 | journal = SIAM Review
 | volume = 51
 | number = 2
 | year = 2009
 | pages = 239–316
 | doi = 10.1137/060671504
 |bibcode = 2009SIAMR..51..239B | arxiv = math/0606118| s2cid = 10435983
 }}</ref>

== Posterior state equations ==
=== Counting observation ===
Let <math>n(t)</math> be a [[Poisson process]] with forward increments <math>dn(t)=0</math> almost everywhere and <math>dn(t)=1</math> otherwise and having the property <math>(dn)^2=dn</math>.  The expected number of events is <math>\mathbb{E}\{n(t)\}=\nu t</math>, where <math>\nu</math> is the expected rate of jumps.  Then substituting <math>m(t)=\frac{n(t)-\nu t}{\sqrt{\nu}}</math> for the stochastic process <math>y(t)</math> gives the linear Belavkin equation for the unnormalized random wavefunction <math>\psi(t,\omega)</math> undergoing counting observation.  Substituting <math>L=\sqrt\nu(C-I)</math>, where <math>C</math> is the collapse operator, and <math>H=E+i\hbar\frac{\nu}{2}(C-C^\ast)</math>, where <math>E</math> is the energy operator, this equation can be written in the following form
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title= 
|equation = :<math>
d\psi=-\left(\frac{\nu}{2}(C^\ast C-I)+\frac{i}{\hbar} E\right)\psi dt+(C-I)\psi dn
</math>
|cellpadding= 6 
|border 
|border colour = #0073CF 
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
Normalized wavefunction <math>\varphi(t,\omega)=\psi(t,\omega)/\|\psi(t,\omega)\|</math> is called the ''posterior state vector'', the evolution of which is described by the following nonlinear equation
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title= 
|equation = :<math>
d\varphi=-\left(\frac{\nu}{2}(C^\ast C-\|C\varphi\|^2)+\frac{i}{\hbar} E\right)\varphi dt+\left(\frac{C}{\|C\varphi\|}-I\right)\varphi d\tilde n
</math>
|cellpadding= 6 
|border 
|border colour = #0073CF 
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
where <math>\tilde n(t)</math> has expectation <math>\mathbb{E}\{\tilde n(t)\}=\nu\|C\varphi\|^2t</math>.  The posterior equation can be written in the standard form
:<math>
d\varphi=-\left(\frac{1}{2} \tilde L^\ast\tilde L+\frac{i}{\hbar}\tilde H\right)\varphi dt+\tilde L\varphi d\tilde m
</math>
with <math>\tilde L=\sqrt\nu(C-\|C\varphi\|)</math>, <math>\tilde H=E+i\hbar\frac{\nu}{2}(C-C^\ast)\|C\varphi\|</math>, and <math>\tilde m(t)=\frac{\tilde n(t)-\nu\|C\varphi\|^2 t}{\sqrt\nu\|C\varphi\|}</math>.  The corresponding equations for the unnormalized random density operator <math>\varrho(t,\omega)=\psi(t,\omega)\psi^\ast(t,\omega)</math> and for the normalized random posterior density operator <math>\rho(t,\omega)=\varphi(t,\omega)\varphi^\ast(t,\omega)</math> are as follows
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title= 
|equation = :<math>
\begin{align}
d\varrho&=-[G\varrho+\varrho G^\ast-\nu\varrho]dt+[C\varrho C^\ast-\varrho]dn\\
d\rho&=-[G\rho+\rho G^\ast-\nu\rho\mathrm{Tr}\left\{C\rho C^\ast\right\}]dt+\left(\frac{C\rho C^\ast}{\mathrm{Tr}\left\{C\rho C^\ast\right\}}-\rho\right)d\tilde n
\end{align}
</math>
|cellpadding= 6 
|border 
|border colour = #0073CF 
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
where <math>G=\frac{\nu}{2} C^\ast C+\frac{i}{\hbar} E</math>.  Note that the latter equation is nonlinear.

=== Continuous observation ===

Stochastic process <math>m(t)</math>, defined in the previous section, has forward increments <math>(dm)^2=\nu^{-1/2}dm+dt</math>, which tend to <math>dt</math> as <math>\nu\to\infty</math>.  Therefore, <math>m(t)</math> becomes standard Wiener process with respect to the input probability measure.  Substituting <math>w(t)</math> for <math>y(t)</math> gives the linear Belavkin equation for the unnormalized random wavefunction <math>\psi(t,\omega)</math> undergoing continuous observation.  The output process <math>\tilde m(t)</math> becomes the diffusion innovation process <math>\tilde w(t)</math> with increments <math>d\tilde w(t,\omega)=dw(t,\omega)-2\mathrm{Re}\langle\varphi(t,\omega)\mid L\varphi(t,\omega)\rangle dt</math>.  The nonlinear Belavkin equation of the diffusion type for the posterior state vector <math>\varphi(t,\omega)=\psi(t,\omega)/\|\psi(t,\omega)\|</math> is
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title= 
|equation = :<math>
d\varphi=-\left(\frac{1}{2} \tilde L^\ast\tilde L+\frac{i}{\hbar}\tilde H\right)\varphi dt+\tilde L\varphi d\tilde w
</math>
|cellpadding= 6 
|border 
|border colour = #0073CF 
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
with <math>\tilde L=L-\mathrm{Re}\langle\varphi\mid L\varphi\rangle</math> and <math>\tilde H=H+i\hbar\frac{1}{2}(L-L^\ast)\mathrm{Re}\langle\varphi\mid L\varphi\rangle</math>.  The corresponding equations for the unnormalized random density operator <math>\varrho(t,\omega)=\psi(t,\omega)\psi^\ast(t,\omega)</math> and for the normalized random posterior density operator <math>\rho(t,\omega)=\varphi(t,\omega)\varphi^\ast(t,\omega)</math> are as follows
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title= 
|equation = :<math>
\begin{align}
  d\varrho&=-[K\varrho+\varrho K^\ast-L\varrho L^\ast]dt+[L\varrho+\varrho L^\ast]dw\\
  d\rho&=-[K\rho+\rho K^\ast-L\rho L^\ast]dt+[L\rho+\rho L^\ast-\rho\mathrm{Tr}\left\{(L+L^\ast)\rho\right\}]d\tilde w
\end{align}
</math>
|cellpadding= 6 
|border 
|border colour = #0073CF 
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}
where <math>K=\frac{1}{2} L^\ast L+\frac{i}{\hbar} H</math>.  The second equation is nonlinear due to normalization.  Because <math>\mathbb{E}\{dw(t)\}=0</math>, taking the average of these stochastic equations over all <math>\omega</math> leads to the [[Lindblad equation]]
:<math>
\frac{d\rho}{dt}=-[K\rho+\rho K^\ast]+L\rho L^\ast
</math>

== Example: continuous observation of position of a free particle ==

Consider a free particle of mass <math>m</math>.  The [[position operator|position]] and [[momentum operator|momentum]] observables correspond respectively to operators <math>\hat x</math> of multiplication by <math>x</math> and <math>\hat p=(\hbar/i)d/dx</math>.  Making the following substitutions in the Belavkin equation
:<math>
L=\hat x,\qquad H=\frac{\hat p^2}{2m}
</math>
the posterior stochastic equation becomes
:<math>
d\varphi=-\left(\frac{1}{2}(\hat x-\langle\hat x\rangle)^2+\frac{i}{\hbar}\frac{\hat p^2}{2m}\right)\varphi dt+\Bigl(\hat x-\langle\hat x\rangle\Bigr)\varphi[dy-2\langle\hat x\rangle dt]
</math>
where <math>\langle\hat x\rangle(t)=\mathrm{Tr}\left\{\hat x\rho(t)\right\}</math> is the posterior expectation of <math>\hat x</math>. Motivated by the spontaneous [[collapse theory]] rather than the filtering theory, this equation was also obtained by Diosi,<ref name="Diosi88a">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Diosi | first1 = L.
 | title = Continuous quantum measurement and Itô formalism
 | journal = Phys Lett A
 | volume = 129
 | number = 8–9
 | year = 1988
 | pages = 419–423
 | doi = 10.1016/0375-9601(88)90309-X
|bibcode = 1988PhLA..129..419D | arxiv = 1812.11591
 | s2cid = 118831121
 }}</ref> showing that the measurement noise <math>dy-2\langle\hat x\rangle dt</math> is the increment <math>d\xi</math> of a standard [[Wiener process]]. There are closed-form solutions to this equation,<ref name="Diosi88b">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Diosi | first1 = L.
 | title = Localized solution of simple nonlinear quantum Langevin-equation
 | journal = Phys Lett A
 | volume = 132
 | number = 5
 | year = 1988
 | pages = 233–236
 | doi = 10.1016/0375-9601(88)90555-5
|bibcode = 1988PhLA..132..233D }}</ref>  as well as equations for a particle in a linear or quadratic potentials.<ref name="Belavkin88" /><ref name="Belavkin89b" /><ref name="Belavkin_Staszewski92">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Belavkin | first1 = V.P.
 | last2 = Staszewski | first2 = P.
 | title = Nondemolition observation of a free quantum particle
 | journal = Physical Review A
 | volume = 45
 | number = 3
 | year = 1992
 | pages = 1347–1357
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevA.45.1347
 | pmid=9907114
|bibcode = 1992PhRvA..45.1347B | arxiv = quant-ph/0512138| s2cid = 14637898
 }}</ref>  For a Gaussian initial state <math>\psi_0</math> these solutions correspond to optimal quantum linear filter.<ref name="Belavkin80" />  Solutions to the Belavkin equation show that in the limit <math>t\to\infty</math> the wavefunction has finite dispersion,<ref name="Kolokoltsov95">{{cite journal
 | last = Kolokol'tsov1 | first = V.N.
 | title = Scattering theory for the Belavkin equation describing a quantum particle with continuously observed coordinate
 | journal = Journal of Mathematical Physics
 | volume = 36
 | number = 6
 | year = 1995
 | pages = 2741–2760
 | doi = 10.1063/1.531063 
|bibcode = 1995JMP....36.2741K }}</ref> therefore resolving the [[quantum Zeno effect]].<ref name="Holevo91" />
